groups.title: Cooling cities with green roofs
groups.passage: Green roofs are not simply gardens placed on top of buildings. A shallow layer of plants and soil can lower the temperature of a roof in summer, while the soil slows rainwater as it runs towards drains. Researchers in one city found that buildings with green roofs used less energy for cooling during hot weeks. The benefits are not identical everywhere: a roof needs enough sunlight, and older structures may need strengthening before soil is added. For this reason, planners often begin with public buildings, where access is easier. Some roofs are designed for wildlife, but many are not open to visitors because their surfaces must be protected. Green roofs therefore work best as part of a wider plan rather than as a single answer to urban heat.

items.stem: What is the main purpose of the passage?
opts: To explain how green roofs can help cities and what limits them
To compare the prices of different roofs
To argue that all city roofs should be opened to visitors
To describe a tour of a public building
items.expl: The passage explains cooling and water benefits, then notes sunlight, structural and access limits.

items.stem: How does the soil on a green roof help during rain?
opts: It removes the need for drains
It slows water on its way to drains
It changes rainwater into drinking water
It directs water into the building
items.expl: The passage says the soil slows rainwater as it runs towards drains.

items.stem: What can be inferred about many wildlife-friendly roofs?
opts: They are always on old buildings
They are not usually available for visitors
items.expl: The passage says many roofs designed for wildlife are not open to visitors because their surfaces need protection.

items.stem: In the passage, what does “shallow” mean?
items.expl: A shallow layer has little depth, so it is not deep.

items.stem: Why may planners start with public buildings?
opts: They are always open at night
items.expl: The passage directly gives easier access as the reason for starting with public buildings.

groups.title: The repair café movement
groups.passage: Repair cafés bring volunteers and local residents together to fix household objects that might otherwise be thrown away. A visitor may arrive with a lamp, a jacket or a small appliance, while a volunteer provides advice and basic tools. The aim is not to offer a free replacement service. Visitors are encouraged to take part so that they understand the fault and can make a similar repair later. Many groups also record the objects they save, which helps them show how much waste they divert from landfill. Repair cafés cannot solve every problem: some electrical faults are unsafe for beginners, and a missing part may be impossible to obtain. Even so, the meetings create a social benefit. People who would not normally meet exchange practical knowledge while extending the life of ordinary possessions.

items.stem: What is the main aim of a repair café?
opts: To teach people to repair items and reduce waste
To collect objects for a museum
items.expl: Visitors join repairs, learn from volunteers and help keep objects out of landfill.

items.stem: What are visitors encouraged to do?
items.expl: The passage says visitors are encouraged to take part so they understand the fault.

items.stem: Why do some groups record the objects they save?
opts: To decide which volunteers may attend
To demonstrate the amount of waste diverted
To calculate the price of a new lamp
items.expl: Records help groups show how much waste they divert from landfill.

items.stem: Which problem is mentioned as a limitation?
opts: Landfill sites are too far away
Some electrical faults may be unsafe
items.expl: The passage warns that some electrical faults are unsafe for beginners.

items.stem: What social effect do repair cafés have?
opts: They make ordinary possessions less useful
They bring people together to exchange knowledge
They stop people from learning practical skills
items.expl: The final sentence says people meet and exchange practical knowledge.

groups.title: Trees and the urban climate
groups.passage: A row of street trees can do more than make a road attractive. Leaves provide shade, and water released from them can cool the air on warm days. Trees also slow rain before it reaches paved surfaces, where water often runs quickly into drains. However, planting a tree is not a complete climate policy. The wrong species may damage pavements with its roots, while a young tree needs several years of watering before it can provide much shade. City workers therefore need to match trees to soil, space and local weather. In some neighbourhoods, residents help by watering new trees and reporting damage. This shared care matters because a tree lost in its first year represents wasted work as well as a lost future benefit.

items.stem: Which benefit of trees is mentioned?
opts: They can shade streets and cool air
They remove the need for city workers
items.expl: The passage mentions shade and cooling from water released by leaves.

items.stem: Why can paved surfaces increase rainwater flow?
items.expl: The passage contrasts soil with paved surfaces, where water often runs quickly into drains.

items.stem: What must city workers consider when choosing trees?
opts: How quickly a tree can be cut down
Only the colour of the leaves
Soil, available space and local weather
items.expl: The passage lists soil, space and local weather as the factors to match.

items.stem: Why is a young tree watered for several years?
opts: To help it provide future shade
To prevent it from having roots
items.expl: A young tree needs watering before it can provide much shade, so care supports its future benefit.

items.stem: In the final sentence, what does “shared care” refer to?
opts: Residents watering trees and reporting damage
items.expl: It refers to residents helping with watering and damage reports.

groups.title: Why people ferment food
groups.passage: Fermentation is an old way of changing food through the activity of microorganisms. In vegetables, these organisms can produce acids that make the food taste sharp and slow the growth of some harmful microbes. Fermentation does not mean that a food will remain safe forever. Clean containers, suitable salt levels and cool storage may still be necessary, depending on the recipe. The process also creates flavours that cannot be produced by simply heating a food. This is one reason why fermented products appear in many culinary traditions, from sour vegetables to cultured milk. Modern cooks sometimes use controlled temperatures to make results more consistent, but the basic principle remains similar to methods used in home kitchens for generations.

items.stem: What causes food to change during fermentation?
items.expl: The first sentence identifies microorganisms as the cause of the change.

items.stem: What can acids produced in fermented vegetables do?
opts: Remove the need for clean containers
Make the food taste less sharp
items.expl: The passage says acids make the taste sharp and slow the growth of some harmful microbes.

items.stem: What does the passage warn about fermentation?
opts: It always requires a modern machine
It does not remove every safety concern
It can only be used for milk
items.expl: The passage directly says fermentation does not mean food remains safe forever.

items.stem: Why do modern cooks sometimes control temperature?
opts: To replace salt in every recipe
items.expl: Controlled temperature is mentioned as a way to make results more consistent.

items.stem: The word “cultured” in the passage is closest in meaning to:
items.expl: In cultured milk, microorganisms are used to change the milk.

groups.title: Restoring mangrove edges
groups.passage: Mangroves grow where rivers meet the sea and their tangled roots hold soft coastal soil in place. They also provide shelter for young fish and reduce the force of waves during storms. Restoration projects do not simply plant as many trees as possible. Teams first examine tides, water channels and the species that were present before the area was damaged. If a blocked channel is left unchanged, new seedlings may be flooded too often or receive too little water. Local residents can help monitor the shore and protect young plants from animals or accidental trampling. A restored mangrove may take years to become a complex habitat, so success is measured through survival and new growth rather than by the number of seedlings planted on the first day.

items.stem: Where do mangroves commonly grow?
items.expl: The passage opens by locating mangroves where rivers meet the sea.

items.stem: What do mangrove roots help to do?
opts: Remove young fish from the shore
items.expl: Their tangled roots hold soft coastal soil in place.

items.stem: Why do restoration teams examine water channels?
opts: Channels are used to count storms
Channels determine whether seedlings get suitable water
Channels show the age of local residents
items.expl: A blocked channel can leave seedlings too wet or too dry, so water flow must be examined.

items.stem: How can local residents support a restoration project?
opts: By monitoring the shore and protecting young plants
By measuring only the first day's planting
items.expl: The passage gives monitoring and protecting young plants as ways residents can help.

items.stem: How is long-term success measured?
opts: By plant survival and new growth
By the colour of the water
By the number of workers hired
By the length of the first meeting
items.expl: The final sentence contrasts survival and new growth with the first-day seedling count.

groups.title: Libraries of things
groups.passage: Some public libraries now lend useful objects as well as books. A library of things may offer sewing machines, camping equipment or tools for home repairs. The service is intended for people who need an item occasionally but do not want to buy and store it permanently. Members usually borrow objects for a limited period and return them so others can use them. This model can save money and reduce the number of rarely used products in homes. It also requires careful management. Staff must check that objects are safe, explain how unfamiliar equipment works and replace missing parts. Libraries do not lend every object: items that are too dangerous, fragile or difficult to maintain are usually excluded. The scheme succeeds when borrowing is convenient and responsibility is shared.

items.stem: Why might someone use a library of things?
opts: They read no books at all
They want to buy more storage space
They need an item only occasionally
They want to keep tools permanently
items.expl: The service is for people who need an item occasionally without buying and storing it.

items.stem: How does the model help reduce products in homes?
opts: One borrowed item can be used by many people
Every member receives a new product
It encourages people to discard working tools
items.expl: An object is returned and shared instead of being bought by each person.

items.stem: What must staff do with unfamiliar equipment?
items.expl: Staff must explain how unfamiliar equipment works.

items.stem: Which objects are usually excluded?
opts: Objects that are dangerous or hard to maintain
items.expl: The passage excludes objects that are too dangerous, fragile or difficult to maintain.

items.stem: According to the passage, what supports the scheme?
items.expl: The final sentence names convenience and shared responsibility as conditions for success.

groups.title: Evening light and sleep
groups.passage: Light helps the human body keep track of day and night. Bright light in the morning can support alertness, while darkness in the evening tells the body that rest is approaching. This does not mean that every lamp or screen has the same effect. The intensity, timing and distance of a light source all matter. A person reading a dim book light may receive less light than someone sitting close to a bright screen. Researchers therefore advise people to consider the whole evening environment rather than blame one device. Keeping a regular bedtime, reducing strong light before sleep and getting daylight during the day are simple habits that may help. They cannot replace medical advice for persistent sleep problems, but they can make the daily pattern of light more predictable.

items.stem: What role can morning light play?
opts: It removes the need for darkness
items.expl: The passage says bright morning light can support alertness.

items.stem: Which three features of a light source are said to matter?
items.expl: The passage lists intensity, timing and distance.

items.stem: Why does the passage compare a book light with a screen?
opts: To illustrate how distance and intensity can differ
To prove that books damage sleep
To show that all devices are equally bright
To explain how to repair a screen
items.expl: The comparison shows that a nearby bright screen can provide more light than a dim book light.

items.stem: What does “persistent” sleep trouble mean?
opts: Sleep trouble caused by travel only
items.expl: Persistent means continuing for a long time or repeatedly.

items.stem: Which habit is recommended?
opts: Using the strongest lamp before sleep
items.expl: Getting daylight during the day is one of the simple habits listed.

groups.title: Amateur astronomy
groups.passage: Amateur astronomers contribute to science even when they do not work at an observatory. A small telescope can reveal the changing position of a planet, and a camera can record a brief event that professionals might not see. Many amateurs join organised projects in which observations are checked against reports from other locations. This makes the data more useful than an isolated photograph. Equipment is not the only requirement. Observers need patience, a dark enough site and a record of the time and conditions. Clouds may prevent a planned observation, but a failed evening is not necessarily wasted: it can teach beginners how local weather changes. By sharing careful records rather than dramatic guesses, amateur groups can support research and help the public understand how evidence is collected.

items.stem: How can an amateur astronomer contribute to science?
opts: By working only in a professional observatory
items.expl: The passage describes careful observations and records as useful contributions.

items.stem: Why are observations from several locations useful?
opts: They remove the need to record time
They can be checked against one another
items.expl: Organised projects compare reports from different locations.

items.stem: Which condition does an observer need?
items.expl: The passage lists a dark enough site among the requirements.

items.stem: What can a failed observing evening teach beginners?
items.expl: The passage says a failed evening can teach beginners about local weather.

items.stem: What contrast does the final sentence make?
opts: Careful records are better than dramatic guesses
items.expl: The final sentence contrasts careful records with dramatic guesses.

groups.title: Small renewable grids
groups.passage: A small renewable grid links local electricity users with sources such as solar panels, batteries and sometimes a wind turbine. It can continue supplying essential buildings when a larger network is interrupted, provided that demand is managed carefully. A school might use stored energy for lights and communications, while postponing less urgent activities. The system is not automatically independent of the national grid. On cloudy days or during a long calm period, it may need additional power, and batteries have a limited capacity. Engineers therefore study local weather and patterns of use before choosing equipment. The value of a small grid is its flexibility: it can reduce pressure on the wider network and help a community practise responding to interruptions, even when it cannot provide every unit of electricity on its own.

items.stem: What can a small renewable grid do during a larger network interruption?
opts: Remove all batteries from the system
Supply essential buildings if demand is managed
items.expl: The passage says it can continue supplying essential buildings when demand is managed carefully.

items.stem: Why might a school postpone some activities?
opts: To use stored energy for less important tasks first
To save stored energy for lights and communication
Because solar panels cannot produce any power
Because the national grid is always available
items.expl: The example says stored energy is used for lights and communications while less urgent activities are postponed.

items.stem: What limits the system's ability to work alone?
opts: Cloudy weather and limited battery capacity
The existence of a wind turbine
items.expl: Cloudy days can reduce generation, and batteries have limited capacity.

items.stem: What do engineers study before choosing equipment?
opts: Only the age of the school
The names of all electricity users
Local weather and patterns of use
items.expl: The passage explicitly names local weather and use patterns.

items.stem: What is the main value of a small grid according to the passage?
opts: Its ability to replace every national network
items.expl: The final sentence identifies flexibility as the value of the system.

groups.title: Making room for urban rivers
groups.passage: For decades, some towns treated rivers as channels to be straightened and hidden beneath roads. More recent projects have taken a different approach: they give a river more room to spread during heavy rain. A wider floodplain can include parks, paths and wetlands that temporarily hold water, reducing pressure on homes downstream. This approach does not mean removing every wall or allowing water to flow wherever it chooses. Engineers still protect bridges and buildings, while planners decide which areas can safely flood. Residents may initially worry that a wetland will look untidy, but native plants can provide habitat and need less maintenance than a formal lawn. The best projects combine flood protection with public space, making the river visible without pretending that flooding can be eliminated completely.

items.stem: What is the newer approach to urban rivers?
opts: Hide every river beneath a road
Give rivers more room during heavy rain
items.expl: The passage contrasts older hidden channels with giving rivers more room to spread.

items.stem: How can a wider floodplain help homes downstream?
opts: It prevents native plants from growing
It temporarily holds water and reduces pressure
It sends all water directly into houses
items.expl: Parks, paths and wetlands in a wider floodplain can temporarily hold water and reduce pressure downstream.

items.stem: What do engineers continue to protect?
items.expl: The passage says engineers still protect bridges and buildings.

items.stem: Why might native plants be useful in a wetland?
opts: They need less maintenance than a formal lawn
items.expl: Native plants can provide habitat and need less maintenance than a formal lawn.

items.stem: What does the final sentence suggest about flooding?
opts: Projects can reduce risk but cannot remove it entirely
It happens only where parks exist
items.expl: The final sentence says good projects do not pretend that flooding can be eliminated completely.
